questions.stem: Why is aluminium chosen for aircraft bodies?

options.text: Its high strength-to-weight ratio, coming from strength combined with low density
options.explanation: Strong but light is exactly what an airframe needs, which is the property listed for aircraft bodies.

options.text: It conducts electricity better than any other metal
options.explanation: Conductivity matters for cables, but the airframe property is strength at low weight.

options.text: It is the cheapest metal available
options.explanation: Cost is not the listed reason; strength with low density is.
options.misconception: cost substituted for the stated property

options.text: It is completely unreactive in every situation
options.explanation: Aluminium is useful because it resists specific attack such as acidic food, not because it never reacts.

questions.stem: Which set of properties makes copper suitable for water pipes?

options.text: Unreactive with water, non-toxic and malleable
options.explanation: These are exactly the three properties listed for water pipes.

options.text: Low density and high strength
options.explanation: Those are aircraft properties for aluminium; pipes need chemical stability and workability.
options.misconception: aluminium properties transferred to copper pipes

options.text: Hardness and a high melting point
options.explanation: Neither property is the listed reason; the pipe must not react with water and must be safe and workable.

options.text: Magnetism and low cost
options.explanation: Copper is not magnetic and cost is not the listed property set.

questions.stem: Which shared property puts both aluminium and copper into saucepans?

options.text: Both are very good conductors of heat
options.explanation: Heat conduction is listed for both metals in the saucepan row.

options.text: Both are ductile enough to be drawn into wires
options.explanation: Ductility is the wiring property; saucepans need heat conduction.

options.text: Both are strongly magnetic
options.explanation: Neither metal is magnetic, and magnetism has no role in cooking.

options.text: Both are the cheapest metals on sale
options.explanation: Cost is not the listed property; conduction of heat is.

questions.stem: Why is aluminium suitable for food cans?

options.text: It is non-toxic and resists corrosion and acidic foodstuffs
options.explanation: The food-can row lists non-toxic behaviour plus resistance to corrosion and acidic foods.

options.text: It conducts electricity so it keeps food warm
options.explanation: Conductivity does not keep food warm and is not the listed reason.

options.text: It is denser than most metals so it seals tightly
options.explanation: Aluminium is prized for low density; the can property is chemical resistance.

options.text: It is magnetic so cans are easy to sort
options.explanation: Sorting convenience is not the listed reason and aluminium is not magnetic.
options.misconception: recycling habit mistaken for the property

questions.stem: Which metal is used for overhead electrical cables, and why?

options.text: Aluminium, because it conducts electricity well and is light
options.explanation: Cables need a good conductor that a pylon can support, and aluminium supplies both.

options.text: Copper, because it is cheaper per metre
options.explanation: Copper wires houses, but overhead cables use aluminium for its conduction at low weight.

options.text: Iron, because it is strong in tension
options.explanation: Strength alone does not qualify; the cable must conduct electricity well.

options.text: Stainless steel, because it resists weathering
options.explanation: Weathering resistance is not the deciding property for the cable conductor.

questions.stem: State the two aluminium properties that suit aircraft bodies.
Which metal is the standard choice for electrical wiring, and which two properties earn it that place?
questions.modelAnswer: Copper: its electrical conductivity and its ductility make it the standard wiring metal.

questions.stem: A can of tomatoes sits on the shelf for months, and the fruit inside is acidic. Explain why the aluminium can survives the acidic food.
questions.modelAnswer: Aluminium is unreactive and shrugs off acidic foodstuffs, so the can metal does not react with the acid even over long storage.

questions.stem: A new overhead cable run is to be strung across a valley and aluminium is chosen for it. Name the property behind the choice and state what the cable is carrying.
questions.modelAnswer: Aluminium conducts electricity very well, and the cable carries an electric current along the overhead line.

questions.stem: Which type of steel is used for car body panels, and why?

options.text: Mild steel, because it is soft and malleable
options.explanation: Body panels must be pressed into shape, which needs the soft, workable character of low-carbon mild steel.

options.text: High-carbon steel, because panels must be hard
options.explanation: Hardness suits chisels and tools; panels need to be shaped, which mild steel does best.

options.text: Stainless steel, because panels must not rust
options.explanation: Corrosion resistance is the stainless property for cutlery and sinks; panels use mild steel's workability.

options.text: Pure iron, because alloys weaken metals
options.explanation: Car panels use mild steel; alloying is done deliberately to tune properties, not always to weaken.

questions.stem: Which steel type suits tools such as chisels?

options.text: High-carbon steel, which is hard
options.explanation: Cutting edges need hardness, and the 0.5-1.4% carbon content provides exactly that.

options.text: Mild steel, which is soft and malleable
options.explanation: A soft chisel would deform on impact; hardness is the required property.

options.text: Stainless steel, which resists corrosion
options.explanation: Corrosion resistance matters for cutlery and sinks; chisels need hardness.

options.text: Pure iron, which is ductile
options.explanation: Ductility helps shaping, not edge retention; the hard high-carbon steel is chosen.

questions.stem: What is stainless steel alloyed with, and where is it used?

options.text: 20% chromium and 10% nickel, for cutlery, sinks and chemical plants
options.explanation: These are exactly the stainless row's composition and uses, prized for strength and corrosion resistance.

options.text: 0.25% carbon, for car body panels
options.explanation: That is mild steel's composition and use, not stainless.

options.text: 0.5-1.4% carbon, for chisels
options.explanation: That is high-carbon steel, the tool alloy.

options.text: 10% copper, for water pipes
options.explanation: No copper appears in the steel table; pipes are copper's own use.

questions.stem: Why is iron chosen as a building material?

options.text: Good strength, malleability and ductility at a relatively low price
options.explanation: The building-material row lists strength, malleability, ductility and low cost together.

options.text: It conducts heat well, keeping buildings warm
options.explanation: Conduction is a saucepan property; buildings want strength and low cost.

options.text: It never corrodes
options.explanation: Iron rusts readily; the building case rests on strength and price, not corrosion resistance.

options.text: It is the lightest structural metal
options.explanation: Aluminium is the low-density choice; iron is chosen for strength at low cost.

questions.stem: What single factor separates the three named types of steel?

options.text: The elements alloyed with the iron, especially the carbon content
options.explanation: Mild, high-carbon and stainless differ by what is mixed in and how much, which sets soft, hard or corrosion-resistant behaviour.

options.text: The furnace in which each steel was made
options.explanation: The type is defined by composition, not by which furnace produced it.

options.text: The country where the steel was produced
options.explanation: Origin plays no part; composition decides the type.

options.text: The temperature at which each steel is used
options.explanation: Service temperature is not the classification; the alloy content is.

questions.stem: Which steel type suits car body panels, and what carbon content gives it that character?
questions.modelAnswer: Mild steel: its low carbon content of about 0.25% leaves it soft and malleable enough to be pressed into panels.

questions.stem: State the two metals alloyed into stainless steel and the property mix that justifies its use.
questions.modelAnswer: Stainless steel mixes in about 20% chromium and 10% nickel, giving strength together with corrosion resistance.

questions.stem: Mild steel, high-carbon steel and stainless steel behave very differently in the workshop. Explain what single variable produces those differences.
questions.modelAnswer: The carbon content decides the character of the steel — the higher the carbon, the harder the steel — so mild steel (about 0.25% carbon) is soft and workable while high-carbon steel (0.5-1.4% carbon) is hard enough for tools.

questions.stem: A joiner needs a chisel that keeps its cutting edge, and a coachbuilder needs panels that press into shape without cracking. Assign each job its steel type, justifying each with one property word.
questions.modelAnswer: The chisel takes high-carbon steel — hard is the property that keeps a cutting edge (0.5-1.4% carbon); the coachbuilder takes mild steel — soft and malleable panels press without cracking (about 0.25% carbon).
